title: UPDATE: China's Rural Villages Pay Price for AI Push Amid Grid Bottlenecks
summary:
The Financial Times reports that residents of the Chinese countryside are facing adverse effects from Beijing's aggressive rollout of artificial intelligence infrastructure. While the state has expanded power generation, with Inner Mongolia hitting 117GW of wind capacity by June, the physical connection between plants and data hubs remains a bottleneck. A new substation takes three to five years to build, whereas a data hall can be completed in about 12 months.

This buildout supports the "AI Plus" campaign and a directive from President Xi Jinping to coordinate the planning of computing power, electricity, and water supply. To stabilize these foundations, the State Council is promoting "suandian xietong," the coordination of computing power and electricity, to better integrate AI into the real economy. Beijing is managing the rollout through tiered, industry-specific policies designed to balance technical development with security assessments.

算电协同: suandian xietong, coordinating computing power and electricity.

China's State Council, chaired by Premier Li Qiang, heard a progress report on its "AI Plus" campaign on October 16. Xinhua's readout lists "promoting suandian xietong" as one step to strengthen AI's foundation, next to technology breakthroughs, algorithm innovation and more high-quality data.

The readout does not say what the term covers.

I recently wrote about one place where compute waits for power: Ulanqab, a city in Inner Mongolia and a hub for AI data centers. "We look forward to the Dongying 500kV project being completed and put into use soon." On September 3, Xinhua Finance, the financial news service of China's state news agency, published those remarks by the chief engineer of VNET's Ulanqab campus. VNET is one of China's largest data center operators. Dongying is a 500kV substation and line project. As of that report, it was still being built.

I read the term as Beijing listing the link between compute and power among AI's foundations: in Ulanqab, that link runs through a substation. What I am watching is the date Dongying is put into use.

If you build data centers in China, what would you want suandian xietong to cover first: grid connections, power prices or site choice?

selectedTweets.text:
"China's western grid has no such bottleneck." I wrote that in February, when I argued that cheap power was an advantage China held in AI.

I was counting generation. Inner Mongolia had 117GW of wind capacity by June and roughly 130GW of mostly coal-fired plants, the FT reported. David Fishman of The Lantau Group, an energy consultancy, told the FT the region likely had the "largest electricity local oversupply" of any administrative region in the world.

Ulanqab shows the limit one step later, in the substations between a power plant and a data hall.
